items.stem: What do the elders imagine?
options: The chase and rescue of the daughters
A wedding feast held inside the grove
A funeral already held for Oedipus himself
A formal trial of Creon before the chorus

items.stem: Whom do the elders picture rescuing the maidens?
options: Theseus
Creon
Ismene
The robber band

items.stem: Complete the line: “West of white Oea’s _____.”
options: harbour
meadow
scaur
temple

items.stem: Complete the line: “Flashes each _____ bright,”
options: banner
helmet
bridle
sandal

items.stem: What do the elders wish for in lines 1134–1137?
options: Wings to watch the battle from above
A sword to join the fight themselves
A ship to carry Oedipus from Athens
A new king to replace Theseus at once

items.stem: Where do the elders first imagine they might chance to behold the meeting?
options: On the Pythian shore or by the torch-lit bay
Inside the very walls of Thebes itself
At Oedipus's still unnamed future resting-place
On the long road back toward the Argive camp

items.stem: What does the opening picture of a flying foe brought finally to stand suggest?
options: The fleeing captors will be forced to stand and fight
The Theban men have already sailed safely out of Attica
The maidens have already chosen to go of their own free will
The chorus means that the chase will not come to blows at all

items.stem: What is the mood of the ode?
options: Eager and anxious
Bored and already indifferent
Bitter toward Theseus and Athens
Comic at the expense of the maidens

items.stem: Besides Zeus, whom do the elders name in the closing prayer for help?
options: Athenè, Apollo, and the Huntress, sister of Apollo
Creon, the robber band, and the whole Theban State
Ismene, Antigone, and the watching wayfarer alone
The Eumolpidae only, without naming any Olympian god

items.stem: Complete the line: “They will be _____:”
options: welcomed
forgotten
vanquishèd
rewarded

items.stem: Complete the line: “Maidens so ill _____,”
options: rewarded
forgotten
honoured
bestead

items.stem: What does the chorus say a vision tells them they shall soon do?
options: Behold the two maidens again
See Oedipus crowned again in Thebes
Watch Creon take Theseus as a captive
Follow the daughters back toward Thebes in haste

items.stem: Why do the elders mention the torch-lit bay and the priestly Eumolpidae?
options: To set the hoped-for meeting in Athens' own sacred landscape
To announce that the mystic rites have already been betrayed
To claim that Theseus has already reached the Theban gates
To replace the rescue with a new festival at Colonus

items.stem: What is the effect of the questions “Fight they or now prepare / To fight?”
options: They keep the action offstage and uncertain, a hope rather than a report
They prove that the battle has already ended in a Theban victory now
They tell the audience that Theseus has refused to leave the altar yet
They turn the whole ode into a comic delay before a wedding song

items.stem: Who is “Him whose wide floods enring / Earth, the great Ocean-king / Whom Rhea bore”?
options: Poseidon, the sea-god, son of Rhea
Apollo, the hunter named later in the prayer
Theseus, already called the captain of the host
Zeus alone, with no other god beside him

items.stem: Complete the line: “By their kin _____.”
options: honoured
buffeted
welcomed
crowned

items.stem: Complete the line: “To be borne with the speed of the _____,”
options: tide
gale
flame
rumour

items.stem: What does the chorus add by saying the captured maidens have been struck and driven by their own family?
options: Their own kinsman has struck them; the captors are family
A foreign army from Argos has already claimed them
The chorus itself has driven the daughters from the grove
The maidens have struck Theseus's men in the glen

items.stem: What change occurs in the closing address to the wayfarer?
options: Hope begins to be confirmed: an escort with the maids is said to draw near
The chorus announces that the daughters have already been led back to Thebes
Oedipus is told that his death has already come in the grove
Theseus is said to have kept the resting-place hidden from them all

items.stem: What does the catalogue of Pallas and the Ocean-king add to the picture of the riders?
options: It sets the horsemen under Athens' own divine patrons, not under a nameless luck
It replaces Theseus with Poseidon as the one and only rescuer in the ode
It proves that the mystic rites have already been fully told to Thebes
It means the chase will be fought at sea, and not at all on land

items.stem: Complete the line: “Of Zeus, Athenè _____,”
options: unarmoured
unspoken
undefiled
unburied

items.stem: Complete the line: “The friends who watch for thee with false _____,”
options: tribute
presage
silence
armour

items.stem: In this ode, the dread Queen and Maid of the torch-lit bay are best identified as:
options: Demeter and Persephone, whose mystic rites belong to Eleusis
Athenè and Artemis, who are later named in the closing prayer
Antigone and Ismene, already safe and waiting inside the grove
The nymphs who once fostered the robber band back in Thebes

items.stem: What does the closing address claim about the friends who have been watching?
options: Their hope will not prove a false sign, because an escort with the maids is drawing near
They have already failed, and the maidens will not be seen again at all
They must now keep Oedipus's resting-place hidden from everyone there
They should send the wayfarer back to Thebes before nightfall comes

items.stem: What is the effect of stacking “Hear us” and “Hear” as the elders name one god after another?
options: The repeated call makes the prayer urgent and gathers the city's gods into one appeal
The repetition shows that the chorus no longer expects any god to listen now
The lines reduce the ode to a roll of Theban gods only, with no Attic names left
The syntax proves the battle is already over and needs no further help at all

items.stem: What is the effect of setting the mystic rites beside the hoped-for clash with the robber band?
options: The chase is imagined on holy Attic ground, defending sacred land and captives
The chorus admits the rites have already been told to Creon's men
The ode replaces the rescue with a hidden burial already performed
The mystic rites are used to forbid Theseus from leaving the shore
